reading.body:
The Independent Community Bankers of America appears in 8 AI lobbying filings, with 22 lobbyists named across them and two bills, HR 2152 and S 2296, cited in filings from 2025 or later.

The pattern is concentration of personnel rather than of filings. Twelve lobbyists appear on all 8 filings, three on 6, three on 4, and four on 1 or 2. A trade association filing on AI is not a single advocate making a case, it is a standing roster that rotates by filing period. The bills named are few relative to the number of people named, which suggests the filings cluster around a narrow set of measures rather than broad AI activity.

For AI specifically, this is the community bank layer of the policy stack. Community banks are the institutions that would carry AI underwriting, fraud detection, and compliance tooling into small-business and consumer lending, and they are regulated by agencies that write the rules those tools must satisfy. Lobbying here is about the terms under which small institutions can adopt AI, not about building it. That places the constraint at the regulatory and supervisory level rather than at compute or power, which is a different kind of bottleneck than the ones that dominate data center siting.

The data does not say what position the association argued, only that it filed. It does not give dollar amounts, agency targets, or the text of HR 2152 and S 2296. It covers one client of one registrant, so it cannot show whether this pattern holds across the banking trade.
